bibl.title: Repetition priming and repetition suppression: Multiple mechanisms in need of testing

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: In this Discussion Paper, we review four different theoretical proposals that have the potential to link repetition suppression and priming, with a particular focus on a proposal that stimulus repetition affects improved efficiency through enhanced neural synchronization.

span.label: repetition priming and repetition suppression
span.quote: Stimulus repetition in identification tasks leads to improved behavioral performance ("repetition priming") but attenuated neural responses ("repetition suppression") throughout task-engaged cortical regions.

span.label: review
span.quote: Below, we review four of the main theoretical proposals about what form these solutions might take (see also Grill-Spector et al., 2006 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Repetition makes task-engaged cells fire more synchronously even as their average rates fall, so processing becomes more efficient and behaviour improves despite reduced activity.
span.quote: A very different proposal that may help to resolve this puzzle is that as cells are firing at lower overall rates, they are firing more synchronously with one another, leading to more efficient neural processing ( Gilbert, Gotts, Carver, & Martin, 2010 ; Gotts, 2003 ) ( Figure 1C ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Coincident input spikes sum on the receiving cell's membrane before the depolarization decays, so synchronous inputs cross spike threshold more reliably than the same number of asynchronous inputs.
span.quote: Small depolarizations that occur simultaneously (i.e. synchronously) in a receiving cell will be much more likely to sum above the voltage threshold needed to evoke an action potential.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: In the Bayesian alternative, learned top-down predictions inhibit the bottom-up sensory evidence, so the residual prediction error - and hence the measured activity - shrinks with repetition.
span.quote: This process is commonly referred to in the literature on Bayesian networks as "explaining away" (e.g. Pearl, 1988 ), since as the appropriate causes of the sensory evidence are learned, the incorrect causes (i.e. prediction error) are reduced and explained away.

span.label: The favoured synchrony account has been evaluated empirically in very few studies.
span.quote: Despite the promise that the Synchrony model holds for resolving the puzzle of repetition priming and repetition suppression, there are relatively few studies that have evaluated it empirically.

span.label: Neither of the two surviving models has been subjected to a full set of experimental tests.
span.quote: However, the Bayesian Explaining Away model has received experimental support, as well, and neither the Synchrony nor Explaining Away models have been run through a full gauntlet of experimental tests.

span.label: How long-term plasticity would link activity decreases to changes in synchrony is unclear.
span.quote: It is further possible that LTD dominates the changes such that activities will be reduced overall, producing repetition suppression, but how this would relate to changes in synchrony is quite unclear.

span.label: a CONTROL CONDITION against which spike-LFP coherence in the gamma range was compared
span.note: eliminates: that the synchronisation change is a general property of the recording rather than an effect of stimulus repetition
span.quote: Spikes elicited by the test grating were simultaneously more synchronized with the local field potential (LFP) (spike-LFP coherence) in the gamma frequency range (30–80 Hz) relative to a control condition in which the adapting grating was replaced with a random dot patch of matched luminance.

span.label: the extreme form of the Explaining Away account was tested against the observed pattern
span.note: eliminates: that ALL repetition suppression is high-level repetition expectation - the extreme version predicts a pattern the data do not show
span.quote: This would appear to rule out the extreme version of the Explaining Away view in which all repetition suppression effects are explained by relatively high-level repetition expectation.

span.label: processing efficiency
span.quote: clear that this pervasive brain-behavior relationship reflects some form of improved processing efficiency, the exact form that it takes remains elusive

span.label: THE PARADOX IN ONE SENTENCE, and it is a SIGN CONFLICT between two measures of one event: `Stimulus repetition in identification tasks leads to IMPROVED behavioral performance (repetition priming) but ATTENUATED neural responses (repetition suppression).` Behaviour gets better while the brain does less. Every mechanism in this paper exists to make those two facts one fact, and a corpus that recorded only `repetition improves performance` would lose the half that makes it interesting
span.quote: Stimulus repetition in identification tasks leads to improved behavioral performance ("repetition priming") but attenuated neural responses ("repetition suppression") throughout task-engaged cortical regions

span.label: FOUR ACCOUNTS OF ONE RELATIONSHIP, and the review's job is to keep them separate rather than to pick: FACILITATION (activity advanced in time - refuted for the typical case by single-cell recording, which finds firing curves to repeated stimuli SUBSUMED UNDER those to novel ones), SHARPENING (the poorly tuned cells drop out), SYNCHRONY (lower rates, tighter timing), and EXPLAINING AWAY (the Bayesian form of facilitation). Everyone agrees on improved efficiency; `the exact form that it takes remains elusive`
span.quote: we review four different theoretical proposals that have the potential to link repetition suppression and priming, with a particular focus on a proposal that stimulus repetition affects improved efficiency through enhanced neural

span.label: A REVIEW WHOSE VERDICT ON ITS OWN FAVOURITE IS A GAP: `Despite the promise that the Synchrony model holds for resolving the puzzle of repetition priming and repetition suppression, THERE ARE RELATIVELY FEW STUDIES THAT HAVE EVALUATED IT EMPIRICALLY.` The title says the same - `Multiple mechanisms IN NEED OF TESTING`. The contribution is an inventory of untested explanations, and the paper is explicit that its preferred one is preferred on promise rather than on evidence
span.quote: Despite the promise that the Synchrony model holds for resolving the puzzle of repetition priming and repetition suppression, there are relatively few studies that have evaluated it empirically

span.label: contradicts → the Facilitation model (Henson, 2003; James et al., 2000)
span.quote: Having reviewed four basic proposals as to how repetition suppression might afford repetition priming, the only view that we consider definitively ruled out by current data is the Facilitation Model, at least in its existing form.

span.label: replicates → Gilbert et al. (2010)
span.quote: We found that stimulus repetition led to repetition priming in both patients and increases in low-frequency evoked power (1–15 Hz) for virtually all task-engaged electrodes (i.e. those that exhibited significant evoked responses), replicating the basic pattern of Gilbert et al. (2010) .

span.label: builds-on → Gotts (2003) neocortical circuit model
span.quote: In a simplified neocortical circuit model that incorporated biologically proportionate numbers of excitatory and inhibitory cells and short-term plasticity mechanisms, Gotts (2003) showed that it was possible to simultaneously address short-lag repetition suppression and priming effects through enhanced synchronization.

span.label: repetition priming —contrasted-with→ repetition suppression
span.note: differs in: THE DIRECTION EACH MOVES ON THE SAME EVENT - repetition IMPROVES the behavioural measure and ATTENUATES the neural one. Not two phenomena but two readings of one, pointing opposite ways, which is the puzzle the paper's four mechanisms exist to dissolve · strength of the relation: 0.95 — THE RECORD'S REASON FOR EXISTING. `contrasted-with` rather than `distinct-from`: the paper is not separating two things, it is insisting they are one thing measured twice and asking why the signs disagree.

span.label: coherence
span.quote: Like Ghuman et al. (2008) , we also observed increases in phase-locking (LFP-LFP coherence) between task-engaged frontal and temporal electrodes in the alpha (8–12 Hz) and low beta (12–18 Hz) frequency ranges.

span.label: Of the four candidate accounts reviewed, only the Facilitation model is judged definitively ruled out by existing data.
span.quote: Having reviewed four basic proposals as to how repetition suppression might afford repetition priming, the only view that we consider definitively ruled out by current data is the Facilitation Model, at least in its existing form.

span.label: The authors judge the enhanced-synchronization account the most promising of the surviving proposals.
span.quote: At present, we view the Synchrony model as the most promising.

span.label: Their earlier neocortical circuit model reproduced repetition suppression and priming together, with spike synchronization rising as firing rates fell.
span.quote: Importantly, as the model's firing rates decreased with repetition, the synchronization of the spike times simultaneously increased.

span.label: Their preliminary intracranial EEG study in two surgical patients found behavioural priming together with increased low-frequency evoked power at essentially every task-engaged electrode.
span.quote: We found that stimulus repetition led to repetition priming in both patients and increases in low-frequency evoked power (1–15 Hz) for virtually all task-engaged electrodes (i.e. those that exhibited significant evoked responses), replicating the basic pattern of Gilbert et al. (2010) .

span.label: The same intracranial recordings showed increased fronto-temporal phase-locking with repetition, in alpha and low beta bands.
span.quote: Like Ghuman et al. (2008) , we also observed increases in phase-locking (LFP-LFP coherence) between task-engaged frontal and temporal electrodes in the alpha (8–12 Hz) and low beta (12–18 Hz) frequency ranges.

span.label: They propose that the processes producing synchronization and those producing activity decreases may be partly separate, which would explain reported dissociations between repetition suppression and priming.
span.quote: We would tentatively suggest that the mechanisms producing changes in synchronization and those resulting in overall activity decreases may be at least partially independent, possibly explaining the lack of relationship between repetition suppression and repetition priming that has occasionally been observed

span.label: repetition priming
span.quote: When we repeatedly encounter an object in the environment, we become faster and more accurate at identifying it, a phenomenon referred to as "repetition priming" (see Tulving and Schacter, 1990 ; Schacter & Buckner, 1998 , for review).

span.label: repetition suppression
span.quote: While behavioral performance improves with stimulus repetition, neural activity in humans (BOLD fMRI) and monkeys (single-cell firing rates) tends to decrease, a phenomenon often referred to as "repetition suppression" (see Desimone, 1996 ; Henson, 2003 ; Grill-Spector, Henson, & Martin, 2006 , for reviews).

span.label: Facilitation model
span.quote: The "Facilitation" model ( Henson, 2003 ; James, Humphrey, Gati, Menon, & Goodale, 2000 ; James & Gauthier, 2006 ) is perhaps the most straightforward resolution, positing that with repetition, neural activity is advanced in time with a more rapid overall time course (see Figure 1A ).

span.label: Sharpening
span.quote: A second idea, often referred to as "Sharpening" ( Desimone, 1996 ; Wiggs & Martin, 1998 ), holds that while neural activity is decreasing on the average, the decreases are carried mainly by the cells that are poorly tuned and/or weakly responsive to the repeated stimuli with the "best" cells (i.e. most selective/responsive) instead retaining their activity levels ( Figure 1B ).

span.label: explaining away
span.quote: This process is commonly referred to in the literature on Bayesian networks as "explaining away" (e.g. Pearl, 1988 ), since as the appropriate causes of the sensory evidence are learned, the incorrect causes (i.e. prediction error) are reduced and explained away.
